To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
species differences in the regulation and distribution of catecholaminergic neurons correlate with differences in the expression of social behavior.

species differences in TH-ir cell size are consistent with the species differences in ploidity, but species differences in the TH-ir cell numbers are nucleus specific, and the species differences in TH cell number in the SNpc correlate with species differences in the behavior of these species.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural and hormonal mechanisms that underlie the expression of social and reproductive behaviors.
the evolution of behavioral phenotypes and how this evolution relates to changes in neural substrates.
the evolution of behavior and the neural mechanisms that regulate it.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the process of evolution of a novel behavioral phenotype may have involved changes in the underlying catecholaminergic system.

the evolution of behavioral phenotype in whiptails involves changes in the number and/or size of TH-ir neurons, and that the evolution of the parthenogen may have involved the evolution of a novel catecholaminergic system.
the process of evolution of the parthenogen has resulted in changes in the catecholamine system of the brain.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the process of evolution can produce changes in the number and size of catecholaminergic cells, which may underlie species differences in behavior.
the evolution of the parthenogen has involved a shift in the regulation of catecholaminergic cells in the SNpc and a reduction in the number of catecholuminergetic cells in the preoptic area.
the parthenogen has larger TH-ir neurons and fewer TH-ir neurons in certain nuclei.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the neural mechanisms that control social behaviors can change in response to evolutionary pressures, and this change can involve changes in the number and/or size of catecholaminergic neurons in the brain.
species differences in catecholaminergic cells may be an important mechanism in the evolution of behavior, and this mechanism may have played a role in the evolution of parthenogenesis in whiptails.
the process of evolution may be a dynamic one in which the underlying neural substracts change as the behavioral phenotype evolves.
